Introduction: The Evolution of Understanding Southern Italy's Economic Lag

The economic disparity between Northern and Southern Italy has been a defining characteristic of Italy's development trajectory since unification in 1861. Often referred to as the "Southern Question" (Questione Meridionale), this regional divide has been the subject of extensive scholarship in Italian-language literature, with explanations evolving significantly over the decades. Early interpretations focused primarily on geographical and cultural explanations, viewing Southern Italy as inherently less developed due to its climate, traditions, and demographic patterns. These perspectives often framed the North-South divide as a natural, almost cultural, inevitability rather than a product of specific historical and institutional factors.

The post-World War II period brought new analytical frameworks, particularly influenced by the work of economists like Luigi La Rocca and Benedetto Croce, who examined the legacy of colonialism in Southern Italy and its impact on development patterns. This period also saw the emergence of the "Mezzogiorno" concept, which came to represent not just a geographical area but a problematic entity with unique developmental challenges. Over time, Italian scholarship evolved to incorporate more sophisticated economic theories, moving from purely cultural explanations toward analyses of structural economic issues, institutional weaknesses, and policy failures. <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-7-sonnet-20250219">

The literature has progressively recognized that the economic lag in Southern Italy cannot be understood through singular explanations but requires multidimensional approaches that account for historical legacies, institutional quality, human capital formation, regional policy interventions, and global economic integration. This evolution in understanding reflects changing intellectual currents in Italian academia and broader European developmental economics, with contemporary research increasingly focusing on evidence-based policy approaches tailored to the specific needs of Southern regions. <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-7-sonnet-20250219">

Early Explanations in the 1950s-1960s: Colonialism and the "Southern Question"

The early post-war period in Italian scholarship was characterized by a focus on historical and cultural explanations for Southern Italy's economic underdevelopment. During the 1950s-1960s, scholars frequently invoked the concept of the "Southern Question" as a framework for understanding this persistent economic lag. This period saw the consolidation of perspectives that traced Southern Italy's developmental challenges to its colonial past, particularly the region's role as Italy's colonial empire in Africa. <cite id="7646c975-0">As noted by D'Agostino, the literature from this era emphasized how the "colonial mission" contributed to underinvestment in the Mezzogiorno, creating a lasting legacy that shaped industrialization patterns well beyond the colonial period</cite>.

These early explanations often framed the South as a region with inherent cultural and civilizational differences that made modern economic development more challenging. Scholars viewed the Mezzogiorno through a lens of exceptionalism, arguing that its distinct cultural identity—shaped by factors like family structure, localism, and clientelism—created obstacles to economic modernization. This perspective maintained that these cultural traits were incompatible with the rational, individualistic values supposedly necessary for capitalist development. <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-7-sonnet-20250219">

The post-war institutional context also influenced early explanations, as the Italian state's interventionist policies toward the South were seen as both a response to and reinforcement of these perceived cultural deficiencies. Rather than addressing structural economic issues, policy approaches often reflected assumptions about Southern cultural inadequacies, further entrenching the developmental gap. These early frameworks established a narrative that would dominate Italian scholarship for decades, focusing on cultural and historical determinism rather than on economic and institutional factors that would later be identified as critical to understanding the persistent North-South divide. <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-7-sonnet-20250219">

Institutions, Governance, and Policy Failures

In recent decades, Italian-language scholarship has increasingly shifted toward viewing institutional quality and governance structures as primary explanatory factors for Southern Italy's economic lag. This perspective gained significant momentum as researchers began to document substantial differences in governance effectiveness between northern and southern regions. <cite id="e046a23b-0">Recent research demonstrates that "institutional quality differences, including corruption, government effectiveness, regulatory quality, rule of law and accountability can explain differences in productivity that persist across Italian regions"</cite>. These findings suggest that the North-South divide reflects not merely geographic differences but fundamental governance deficiencies in the southern regions.

The impact of institutional quality on economic performance has been quantified through regional panel data analysis, revealing that "the institutional quality has a statistically and economically significant impact on economic performance in regions, and significantly lower returns to institutional changes in the Southern regions." <cite id="e046a23b-0">This research challenges the notion that the persistent economic gap simply results from insufficient investment in the South, arguing instead that "the failure of the policy in Italy cannot be simply attributed to the lack of investment but involves more profound structural and government-related issues"</cite>.

The literature has also examined how weak local institutional involvement has perpetuated development challenges in Southern Italy. Historical analysis has documented "the weak involvement of local institutions" in the region's development, which contributed to ineffective policy implementation and persistent underdevelopment. <cite id="e046a23b-2">This lack of local participation in governance has created a cycle where "the engagement of local authorities in policymaking exacerbated the living conditions in Southern Italy and hindered economic growth"</cite>.

Decentralization policies implemented in 1971 have had complex and largely negative effects on Southern Italy's development trajectory. Rather than improving governance effectiveness, these policies "became a persistent modus operandi in policy implementation and a problem for Southern Italy," often leading to corruption and nepotism that undermined development efforts. <cite id="e046a23b-2">The shift away from direct state intervention in the South, influenced by changing economic paradigms in the 1970s, further complicated governance issues as "regional disparity in Italy went out from the political agenda, leading to a substantial reduction in policies to foster regional convergence"</cite>.

Labor Mobility, Brain Drain, and Regional Disparities

While early scholarship primarily focused on cultural and historical explanations, Italian-language research in recent decades has increasingly highlighted the role of labor mobility patterns in perpetuating Southern Italy's economic lag. Contemporary scholarship recognizes that migration flows, particularly the selective emigration of skilled workers, have created a self-reinforcing cycle of regional disadvantage.

The selective nature of migration from the Mezzogiorno has been identified as a critical factor in reinforcing Italy's dualistic economic structure. Unlike traditional migration patterns that distribute workers across different skill levels, migration from Southern Italy has disproportionately involved highly qualified individuals. This selective emigration "reinforces the dualistic nature of the Italian economy, exacerbating regional inequalities." <cite id="743c99c3-0"></cite>

The phenomenon of "brain drain" has emerged as a particularly significant concern in Italian scholarship, with researchers documenting how the outflow of educated individuals from Southern regions creates lasting developmental challenges. <cite id="743c99c3-1">Between 2013 and 2019, an average of 24.7% of first-level graduates from southern universities enrolled in master's programs in the Centre-North, while only 0.6% moved in the opposite direction</cite>. This substantial outflow of talent represents not just an immediate loss of human capital but a long-term depletion of the South's intellectual resources.

The consequences of this educational migration extend beyond simple human capital losses. Research indicates that these mobility patterns "exacerbate the enduring spatial disparities within Italy" by strengthening the economy of northern provinces through what has been termed a "brain gain" while simultaneously depleting opportunities in southern regions. This creates a territorial cycle where "public policies have, paradoxically, not mitigated but seemingly intensified these disparities, perpetuating a negative cycle of talent outflow and contributing to the competitive advantage of the northern regions." <cite id="743c99c3-0"></cite>

Student mobility represents a particularly concerning dimension of this brain drain phenomenon, as research shows that educational migration flows contribute to widening rather than narrowing regional gaps. <cite id="743c99c3-1">Analysis of student movement patterns demonstrates that "student mobility exacerbates the enduring spatial disparities within Italy," with evidence that "incoming students have a notably positive and significant impact on the economic growth of the province where they study," particularly benefiting Centre-North regions</cite>. This pattern suggests that the educational institutions in southern regions not only fail to retain their graduates but actively contribute to the economic strengthening of northern territories.

Human Capital, Social Pathologies, and Development Deficits

In recent decades, Italian-language scholarship has increasingly emphasized the fundamental role of human capital deficits in perpetuating Southern Italy's economic lag. This perspective has evolved from earlier views that treated educational disparities as secondary factors to a recognition that human capital formation represents a primary driver of regional economic development.

Research has documented how educational disadvantages have created a self-reinforcing cycle of underdevelopment in Southern Italy. <cite id="01517efa-0">Studies have established that "schooling and education are crucial determinants of the long-term economic divergence between the North and the South of the country"</cite>. This understanding has led scholars to view educational disparities not merely as symptoms of the North-South divide but as its fundamental cause.

The literature has also identified how human capital deficits have contributed to broader demographic and social challenges in the South. <cite id="01517efa-1">Italian scholars have recognized that "low education attainment and, more in general, a poor quality of the human capital, high unemployment rate, a perennial 'brain drain' towards the 'north' and the spread of organized crime" collectively contribute to the region's disadvantaged status within the European Union</cite>. This multifaceted approach recognizes the interconnected nature of social and economic challenges in Southern Italy.

The concept of "passive modernization" has emerged in the literature to describe how the South has primarily experienced state-led but less effective development processes. <cite id="01517efa-2">This theory suggests that "in the lack of active modernization, Southern Italy converged thanks to passive modernization, i.e., State intervention," but that these interventions were "more effective in life expectancy, less successful in education, expensive and as a whole ineffective in GDP"</cite>. This perspective highlights how policy approaches have often addressed immediate symptoms rather than building the foundational human capital necessary for sustained economic growth.

Contemporary scholarship has also recognized how these human capital deficits have created demographic feedback loops that further impede development in the South. As noted in the literature, "whereas in the North the higher wages have been able to attract migrants from the South and to maintain a stable fertility rate, in the South the lack of job opportunities has led to declining fertility rates and emigration, thus reinforcing regional disparities." <cite id="01517efa-0">This understanding has prompted more recent research to focus on educational reform and human capital investment as essential components of any comprehensive strategy to address Southern Italy's economic lag</cite>.

Infrastructure Deficits and Development Policies

In recent years, Italian-language scholarship has increasingly recognized infrastructure deficits and development policy failures as critical components in understanding Southern Italy's economic lag. This perspective has emerged as researchers have documented how infrastructure deficiencies have created a persistent cycle of underdevelopment that has proven difficult to overcome despite decades of intervention.

A significant body of research has examined how infrastructure deficits in the South have created additional economic burdens that directly impact regional competitiveness. <cite id="31d17040-0">Studies have documented that "the loss of GDP but also on the mobilisation of private resources to which Italy is the less attractive country" due to infrastructure deficiencies</cite>. These findings suggest that infrastructure deficits create not only immediate economic losses but also discourage private investment, compounding the developmental challenges facing Southern Italy.

The impact of infrastructure deficits has been particularly pronounced in relation to public investment policies. <cite id="31d17040-1">Research demonstrates that "the collapse of public investment observable in Italy over the last decade has penalised southern regions disproportionally, considering these regions' much lower endowment of public infrastructures"</cite>. This analysis highlights how the structural characteristics of Southern Italy—its already disadvantaged starting position—make it particularly vulnerable to reductions in public investment, creating a feedback loop where underinvestment in infrastructure leads to persistent economic disadvantages.

More recent scholarship has examined specific policy approaches to addressing these infrastructure deficits, particularly focusing on the potential of Special Economic Zones (SEZs) as an industrial policy tool. Research has demonstrated that when these policies are properly implemented, they can be effective in reducing regional disparities. <cite id="31d17040-2">Studies of the Puglia region's SEZs show that "the presence of SEZs appears to positively influence regional development" and that "a positive impact that would not have materialized without the policy" has been documented through robust comparative analysis</cite>.

Beyond infrastructure investment, contemporary scholarship has increasingly emphasized the importance of coordinated territorial strategies that address the complex spatial dimensions of the North-South divide. <cite id="31d17040-0">Researchers have argued that "the South must think together and switch off over time" to achieve "critical mass in a strategic vision for the southern regional interconnected and relational system"</cite>. This perspective suggests that effective development policy requires overcoming the "atomization of interventions" that has characterized previous approaches and instead developing integrated strategies that address the interconnected nature of regional development challenges.

Current Perspectives and Future Directions

In recent years, Italian-language scholarship has moved beyond singular-factor explanations toward more comprehensive frameworks that recognize the complex, multidimensional nature of the North-South divide. Contemporary research increasingly emphasizes the importance of place-based policies that acknowledge the unique characteristics and historical contexts of Southern Italian regions rather than applying uniform national approaches. This shift reflects a growing recognition that effective development strategies must be tailored to the specific socioeconomic conditions, cultural contexts, and institutional capacities of individual southern regions.

The literature now more frequently addresses what scholars describe as the "triple divide" facing Italy's southern regions—the simultaneous existence of geographical, urban-rural, and coastal-inland gradients that all correlate with levels of economic development. This more nuanced spatial perspective has prompted researchers to develop more sophisticated analytical frameworks that can capture these complex spatial dynamics. <cite id="e046a23b-2">As noted by recent scholarship, "the spatial distribution of district value added" cannot be understood through "the traditional north-south axis alone," necessitating "at least two additional axes, the coastal-inland and the urban-rural gradients, as associated to the level of economic development"</cite>.

Contemporary Italian research also increasingly emphasizes the importance of regional specialization and comparative advantage as factors that can inform more effective development policies. Rather than viewing the South's economic structure as inherently inferior, this approach recognizes that different regions develop distinctive economic profiles based on their resource endowments, historical trajectories, and institutional contexts. This perspective has led to greater interest in how regional innovation systems in Southern Italy can be strengthened to support locally appropriate economic development paths.

The evolving scholarly consensus suggests that overcoming Southern Italy's economic lag will require integrated approaches that simultaneously address institutional quality, human capital formation, infrastructure deficits, and regional policy coherence. <cite id="e046a23b-2">As recent scholarship emphasizes, "designing 'one-size-fits-some' forms of national industrial policies" has proven ineffective, and instead, "place-based policies" that acknowledge "the key role of geography in shaping economic opportunities" offer a more promising path forward</cite>. This recognition represents a significant shift in emphasis within Italian-language scholarship, moving away from purely national or centralized approaches toward more localized strategies that can better address the specific challenges facing different parts of Southern Italy.

After the 1970s, the economic paradigm shifted, fostering scepticism towards direct economic intervention. In Italy, this shift triggered a heated debate about the activities of CasMez. Consequently, the regional disparity in Italy went out from the political agenda, leading to a substantial reduction in policies to foster regional convergence (Barca et al. 2012). The prevailing belief that CasMez was essentially a waste of resources that did not produce economic development in Southern Italy played a pivotal role in justifying this disengagement. It erected an ideological barrier to public intervention, especially in Southern Italy. The ascension of the right-wing Northern League party, which utilised anecdotal evidence to contend that fiscal resources were being squandered in Southern Italy, further entrenched this prevailing wisdom (Cento Bull 1993). Concurrently, a new player in regional policies emerged: the European Union's structural funds entrusted to local institutions. Regrettably, these policies did not substantially influence Southern Italy's growth; instead, they exacerbated corruption and nepotism (De Angelis et al. 2020;Di Cataldo and Mastrorocco 2022). The root cause of this failure can be traced back to the decentralisation of 1971, which became a persistent modus operandi in policy implementation and a problem for Southern Italy.

Title: The Dynamics of Fund Absorption: Evaluating the Efficacy of EU Structural Funds in Mitigating Regional Inequalities—Calabrian Case
Snippet: Historically, the migratory outflows from the Italian Mezzogiorno have shaped the socio-economic fabric of southern Italy.The 150-year timeline reveals a transition from the predominantly uneducated migrants of the early 20th century to the present-day exodus of educated young adults (Etzo 2011).This shift, particularly evident since the latter half of the 20th century, has been exacerbated by economic crises and a decrease in labor-intensive industries (Bonifazi et al. 2021).Since the 1990s, a resurgence in emigration has been noted, predominantly among those with secondary and higher education, propelled by disparate economic development between the southern regions and the more affluent central and northern Italy (Etzo 2011;Odoardi and Muratore 2019).Today's migratory flows are characterized by the internal and international relocation of individuals seeking superior educational and professional opportunities, contributing to a self-perpetuating cycle of territorial dualism and the enrichment of foreign labor markets at the expense of local development (Aronica et al. 2023;Basile et al. 2019).

The drivers of this migration are multifaceted, with educational and employment opportunities being primary motivators for those seeking regions where their skills are recognized and rewarded (Ferrara et al. 2018).The statistical narrative provided by the Instituto Nazionale di Statistica (ISTAT) for 2018 (ISTAT 2018) delineates a stark portrait of interregional transfers, signifying a substantial migration of the educated populace from the Mezzogiorno to more prosperous regions, further depleting the south's human capital (Statista 2019).

While labor mobility is traditionally seen as a mechanism for economic equilibrium, the Italian scenario deviates from this model due to the selective nature of the migration, which prioritizes highly qualified individuals.This selective emigration, as opposed to a homogenous distribution of workers, reinforces the dualistic nature of the Italian economy, exacerbating regional inequalities (Basile et al. 2019;Ballatore and Mariani 2019).The intervention of public policies has, paradoxically, not mitigated but seemingly intensified these disparities, perpetuating a negative cycle of talent outflow and contributing to the competitive advantage of the northern regions (Coniglio and Prota 2017).

Title: Brain gain versus brain drain: the effects of universities’ mobile students on territorial inequalities
Snippet: Between 2013 and 2019, an average of 24.7% of first-level graduates from southern universities enrolled in a master's degree in the Centre-North, while only 0.6% of graduates moved in the opposite direction. This graduate outflow phenomenon is especially relevant for southern regions' local development considering that a large share of these mobile students, once graduated, integrate into the local workforce (Alma-Laurea, 2021), strengthening the economy of the northern provinces (brain gain) while simultaneously depleting opportunities in the southern regions (brain drain). Consequently, student mobility exacerbates the enduring spatial disparities within Italy. 

Thus, a more specific research question is to investigate the spatial inequalities generated by student mobility. Accordingly, we analyse the impact of both incoming and outgoing students on the gross domestic product (GDP) per capita growth rate of Italian NUTS-3 regions. Furthermore, we assess whether the northern provinces benefit from a brain gain instead of a brain drain suffered by the southern areas due to student outflows. Lastly, we compute the additional contribution of student mobility to the existing income gap between the South and the Centre-North of Italy over the considered period. 

Another novelty of our analysis is that we focus on the mobility flows of students who have completed a first-level degree and chosen to pursue a second-level degree in a different Italian province. Section 3.1 provides a detailed definition of these mobile students. Unlike Ballarino et al. (2022), who examine first-level students, we concentrate on second-level students because they are closer to entering the labour market and, therefore, have a more immediate impact on the economic performance of the destination region (Dotti et al., 2013). 

The empirical model is based on a standard fixed effects growth model where the province's per capita GDP growth rate depends on the inflows and outflows of mobile students while controlling for other characteristics of the local economy, such as resident students, initial GDP conditions and population density. 

Our results show that in Italy incoming students have a notably positive and significant impact on the economic growth of the province where they study. This effect is especially pronounced in the Centre-North regions, where the influx of students contributes to a 'brain gain' phenomenon.

Title: A “Silent Revolution”: school reforms and Italy’s educational gender gap in the Liberal Age (1861–1921)
Snippet: Italy's economic growth in the long run is tightly linked to human capital accumulation. Vasta (1999) maintains that the remarkable delay in human capital accumulation has been a heavy toll on the country's capability to reach sustained growth in the long run and up to the present day (Di Martino and Vasta 2017). Indeed, the new stream of empirical quantitative studies in Italy's economic history has claimed that the aggregate stock of human capital is a main driver of industrial location (Basile andCiccarelli 2018, Missiaia 2018), innovation (Nuvolari and Vasta 2017), industrial growth (Cappelli 2017a) and the growth of real wages (Federico et al. 2019). 

Furthermore, schooling and education are crucial determinants of the long-term economic divergence between the North and the South of the country (Felice 2012;Felice and Vasta 2015). 

Due to this line of research, Italy's primary-school system during the Liberal Age and its relationship with education and human capital accumulation have been debated extensively, being mainly focused on the country's comparative human capital disadvantage and the educational North-South divide. Within the literature, there is a general agreement on the problematic nature of Italy's decentralized primary-school system (Felice and Vasta 2015;Cappelli 2017b), which hampered human capital accumulation, innovation and technological progress (Nuvolari andVasta 2015, 2017). As we explain in more detail below, the system established in 1859 set forth that funding and management of primary schooling was a burden on Italy's municipalities. New legislation on primary education in the first decade of the twentieth century-such as the Coppino or the Orlando Laws-produced a reduction in the literacy divide between North and South and prompted more rapid human capital formation; yet, amazingly, by 1911, average adult male literacy in the South was no higher than what it had been in Northern Italy in 1821 (Ciccarelli and Weisdorf 2019; Figure 7) and Italy lagged behind the educational performance of other countries. 

Two main interpretations have been provided on the determinants of such educational trends.

Italy's experience suggests that northern Italy's export-led regions have managed to cope with greater global competition and a 'hard-currency' monetary regime in Europe. Indeed, as of 2022, Italy accounted 5 for 19 per cent of total EU industrial production, second only to Germany (at 26 per cent). Thus, thirty years after Richard Locke's writings (Locke 1995), Italy is still characterised by a dysfunctional national political economy hiding resilient patterns of regional economic dynamism. On the contrary, the sheltered AK regions of southern Italy have suffered disproportionately from the Eurozone's fiscal constraints and the austerity measures implemented after Italy's sovereign debt crisis. Given the key compensatory role played by public employment in AK regions, the public sector wage freezes and cuts implemented during 2009-2016(Di Carlo 2023) have eroded southern households' capacity to consume, further depressing regional demand and growth in AK regions. Likewise, the collapse of public investment observable in Italy over the last decade has penalised southern regions disproportionally, considering these regions' much lower endowment of public infrastructures (SVIMEZ 2023, p. XVI). Thus, taking regional growth regimes into account points to a more differentiated impact of European integration across heterogeneous territories within national models of capitalism. 

Thirdly, unearthing and understanding the structural differences across regions' growth regimes shall be instrumental for the design of place-based policies to avoid designing 'one-size-fits-some' forms of national industrial policies. Related to these aspects, through regional input-output data, future CPE research could also investigate the interlinkages between regional growth models to analyse intra-country patterns of regional trade and value chains and detect complementarities between regional growth regimes. 

Considering that the topic addressed in this article is politically contentious in Italy, we conclude by stressing that our analysis carries no normative judgement against southern Italy's 'subsidised' growth regime. Our aim was simply to analyse the ideal-typical characteristics of Italy's regional growth regimes.

Title: Are Special Economic Zone policies (SEZ) effective? An empirical analysis on the transport and logistics’ sector
Snippet: To attract investment, stimulate economic growth, and generate employment, many countries have established SEZs. These areas offer fiscal benefits and receive financial, infrastructural, and logistical support while governed by special legislation and streamlined procedures distinct from other parts of the country. Generally, these zones have proven to be effective industrial policy tools, driving economic growth at both national and local levels. However, their success ultimately hinges on the long-term objectives of the associated industrial policies (Arbolino, Lantz, and Napolitano 2023). Aligning instruments such as the SEZs in Southern Italy with the substantial resources provided by the PNRR could represent a strategic combination capable of reducing productive and social disparities between the South and the more developed central-northern regions (Di Berardino et al. 2016). 

Previous studies have highlighted that the SEZs in Puglia have destinated significant resources into transport and logistics (Nisticò and Prota 2023). Although the literature acknowledges that policy impacts vary by region and, in some cases, have a very limited impact on firms in the service sector (Frick and Rodríguez-Pose 2022;Rodríguez-Pose et al. 2022), this analysis of Puglia offers counterintuitive results demonstrating that effective integration of SEZ policies is heavily dependent on the local economic context. Our findings reveal that the introduction of SEZs in Puglia has led to an increase of more than 10% on average in the turnover of transport sector companies. These results highlight the significance of industrial policy and support the ongoing evolution of SEZ policy in Italy, which is culminating in the establishment of a unified SEZ for the South of Italy. Under this new model, previously limited to select territories, fiscal and administrative benefits will be accessible to all companies in the Southern Regions. 

Additionally, this study enhances the understanding of the link between SEZs and regional growth in Italy. For Puglia, the presence of SEZs appears to positively influence regional development. It also addresses scepticism regarding the effectiveness of SEZs. By employing a robust control group, we demonstrate a positive impact that would not have materialized without the policy, offering encouraging evidence for policymakers about the effectiveness of SEZs.

Introduction: The Evolution of Understanding Southern Italy's Economic Lag

The economic disparity between Northern and Southern Italy has been a defining characteristic of Italy's development trajectory since unification in 1861. Often referred to as the "Southern Question" (Questione Meridionale), this regional divide has been the subject of extensive scholarship in Italian-language literature, with explanations evolving significantly over the decades. Early interpretations focused primarily on geographical and cultural explanations, viewing Southern Italy as inherently less developed due to its climate, traditions, and demographic patterns. These perspectives often framed the North-South divide as a natural, almost cultural, inevitability rather than a product of specific historical and institutional factors.

The post-World War II period brought new analytical frameworks, particularly influenced by the work of economists like Luigi La Rocca and Benedetto Croce, who examined the legacy of colonialism in Southern Italy and its impact on development patterns. This period also saw the emergence of the "Mezzogiorno" concept, which came to represent not just a geographical area but a problematic entity with unique developmental challenges. Over time, Italian scholarship evolved to incorporate more sophisticated economic theories, moving from purely cultural explanations toward analyses of structural economic issues, institutional weaknesses, and policy failures. <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-7-sonnet-20250219">

The literature has progressively recognized that the economic lag in Southern Italy cannot be understood through singular explanations but requires multidimensional approaches that account for historical legacies, institutional quality, human capital formation, regional policy interventions, and global economic integration. This evolution in understanding reflects changing intellectual currents in Italian academia and broader European developmental economics, with contemporary research increasingly focusing on evidence-based policy approaches tailored to the specific needs of Southern regions. <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-7-sonnet-20250219">

Early Explanations in the 1950s-1960s: Colonialism and the "Southern Question"

The early post-war period in Italian scholarship was characterized by a focus on historical and cultural explanations for Southern Italy's economic underdevelopment. During the 1950s-1960s, scholars frequently invoked the concept of the "Southern Question" as a framework for understanding this persistent economic lag. This period saw the consolidation of perspectives that traced Southern Italy's developmental challenges to its colonial past, particularly the region's role as Italy's colonial empire in Africa. <cite id="7646c975-0">As noted by D'Agostino, the literature from this era emphasized how the "colonial mission" contributed to underinvestment in the Mezzogiorno, creating a lasting legacy that shaped industrialization patterns well beyond the colonial period</cite>.

These early explanations often framed the South as a region with inherent cultural and civilizational differences that made modern economic development more challenging. Scholars viewed the Mezzogiorno through a lens of exceptionalism, arguing that its distinct cultural identity—shaped by factors like family structure, localism, and clientelism—created obstacles to economic modernization. This perspective maintained that these cultural traits were incompatible with the rational, individualistic values supposedly necessary for capitalist development. <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-7-sonnet-20250219">

The post-war institutional context also influenced early explanations, as the Italian state's interventionist policies toward the South were seen as both a response to and reinforcement of these perceived cultural deficiencies. Rather than addressing structural economic issues, policy approaches often reflected assumptions about Southern cultural inadequacies, further entrenching the developmental gap. These early frameworks established a narrative that would dominate Italian scholarship for decades, focusing on cultural and historical determinism rather than on economic and institutional factors that would later be identified as critical to understanding the persistent North-South divide. <Model name="Anthropic" version="claude-3-7-sonnet-20250219">

Institutions, Governance, and Policy Failures

In recent decades, Italian-language scholarship has increasingly shifted toward viewing institutional quality and governance structures as primary explanatory factors for Southern Italy's economic lag. This perspective gained significant momentum as researchers began to document substantial differences in governance effectiveness between northern and southern regions. <cite id="e046a23b-0">Recent research demonstrates that "institutional quality differences, including corruption, government effectiveness, regulatory quality, rule of law and accountability can explain differences in productivity that persist across Italian regions"</cite>. These findings suggest that the North-South divide reflects not merely geographic differences but fundamental governance deficiencies in the southern regions.

The impact of institutional quality on economic performance has been quantified through regional panel data analysis, revealing that "the institutional quality has a statistically and economically significant impact on economic performance in regions, and significantly lower returns to institutional changes in the Southern regions." <cite id="e046a23b-0">This research challenges the notion that the persistent economic gap simply results from insufficient investment in the South, arguing instead that "the failure of the policy in Italy cannot be simply attributed to the lack of investment but involves more profound structural and government-related issues"</cite>.

The literature has also examined how weak local institutional involvement has perpetuated development challenges in Southern Italy. Historical analysis has documented "the weak involvement of local institutions" in the region's development, which contributed to ineffective policy implementation and persistent underdevelopment. <cite id="e046a23b-2">This lack of local participation in governance has created a cycle where "the engagement of local authorities in policymaking exacerbated the living conditions in Southern Italy and hindered economic growth"</cite>.

Decentralization policies implemented in 1971 have had complex and largely negative effects on Southern Italy's development trajectory. Rather than improving governance effectiveness, these policies "became a persistent modus operandi in policy implementation and a problem for Southern Italy," often leading to corruption and nepotism that undermined development efforts. <cite id="e046a23b-2">The shift away from direct state intervention in the South, influenced by changing economic paradigms in the 1970s, further complicated governance issues as "regional disparity in Italy went out from the political agenda, leading to a substantial reduction in policies to foster regional convergence"</cite>.

Labor Mobility, Brain Drain, and Regional Disparities

While early scholarship primarily focused on cultural and historical explanations, Italian-language research in recent decades has increasingly highlighted the role of labor mobility patterns in perpetuating Southern Italy's economic lag. Contemporary scholarship recognizes that migration flows, particularly the selective emigration of skilled workers, have created a self-reinforcing cycle of regional disadvantage.

The selective nature of migration from the Mezzogiorno has been identified as a critical factor in reinforcing Italy's dualistic economic structure. Unlike traditional migration patterns that distribute workers across different skill levels, migration from Southern Italy has disproportionately involved highly qualified individuals. This selective emigration "reinforces the dualistic nature of the Italian economy, exacerbating regional inequalities." <cite id="743c99c3-0"></cite>

The phenomenon of "brain drain" has emerged as a particularly significant concern in Italian scholarship, with researchers documenting how the outflow of educated individuals from Southern regions creates lasting developmental challenges. <cite id="743c99c3-1">Between 2013 and 2019, an average of 24.7% of first-level graduates from southern universities enrolled in master's programs in the Centre-North, while only 0.6% moved in the opposite direction</cite>. This substantial outflow of talent represents not just an immediate loss of human capital but a long-term depletion of the South's intellectual resources.

The consequences of this educational migration extend beyond simple human capital losses. Research indicates that these mobility patterns "exacerbate the enduring spatial disparities within Italy" by strengthening the economy of northern provinces through what has been termed a "brain gain" while simultaneously depleting opportunities in southern regions. This creates a territorial cycle where "public policies have, paradoxically, not mitigated but seemingly intensified these disparities, perpetuating a negative cycle of talent outflow and contributing to the competitive advantage of the northern regions." <cite id="743c99c3-0"></cite>

Student mobility represents a particularly concerning dimension of this brain drain phenomenon, as research shows that educational migration flows contribute to widening rather than narrowing regional gaps. <cite id="743c99c3-1">Analysis of student movement patterns demonstrates that "student mobility exacerbates the enduring spatial disparities within Italy," with evidence that "incoming students have a notably positive and significant impact on the economic growth of the province where they study," particularly benefiting Centre-North regions</cite>. This pattern suggests that the educational institutions in southern regions not only fail to retain their graduates but actively contribute to the economic strengthening of northern territories.

Human Capital, Social Pathologies, and Development Deficits

In recent decades, Italian-language scholarship has increasingly emphasized the fundamental role of human capital deficits in perpetuating Southern Italy's economic lag. This perspective has evolved from earlier views that treated educational disparities as secondary factors to a recognition that human capital formation represents a primary driver of regional economic development.

Research has documented how educational disadvantages have created a self-reinforcing cycle of underdevelopment in Southern Italy. <cite id="01517efa-0">Studies have established that "schooling and education are crucial determinants of the long-term economic divergence between the North and the South of the country"</cite>. This understanding has led scholars to view educational disparities not merely as symptoms of the North-South divide but as its fundamental cause.

The literature has also identified how human capital deficits have contributed to broader demographic and social challenges in the South. <cite id="01517efa-1">Italian scholars have recognized that "low education attainment and, more in general, a poor quality of the human capital, high unemployment rate, a perennial 'brain drain' towards the 'north' and the spread of organized crime" collectively contribute to the region's disadvantaged status within the European Union</cite>. This multifaceted approach recognizes the interconnected nature of social and economic challenges in Southern Italy.

The concept of "passive modernization" has emerged in the literature to describe how the South has primarily experienced state-led but less effective development processes. <cite id="01517efa-2">This theory suggests that "in the lack of active modernization, Southern Italy converged thanks to passive modernization, i.e., State intervention," but that these interventions were "more effective in life expectancy, less successful in education, expensive and as a whole ineffective in GDP"</cite>. This perspective highlights how policy approaches have often addressed immediate symptoms rather than building the foundational human capital necessary for sustained economic growth.

Contemporary scholarship has also recognized how these human capital deficits have created demographic feedback loops that further impede development in the South. As noted in the literature, "whereas in the North the higher wages have been able to attract migrants from the South and to maintain a stable fertility rate, in the South the lack of job opportunities has led to declining fertility rates and emigration, thus reinforcing regional disparities." <cite id="01517efa-0">This understanding has prompted more recent research to focus on educational reform and human capital investment as essential components of any comprehensive strategy to address Southern Italy's economic lag</cite>.

Infrastructure Deficits and Development Policies

In recent years, Italian-language scholarship has increasingly recognized infrastructure deficits and development policy failures as critical components in understanding Southern Italy's economic lag. This perspective has emerged as researchers have documented how infrastructure deficiencies have created a persistent cycle of underdevelopment that has proven difficult to overcome despite decades of intervention.

A significant body of research has examined how infrastructure deficits in the South have created additional economic burdens that directly impact regional competitiveness. <cite id="31d17040-0">Studies have documented that "the loss of GDP but also on the mobilisation of private resources to which Italy is the less attractive country" due to infrastructure deficiencies</cite>. These findings suggest that infrastructure deficits create not only immediate economic losses but also discourage private investment, compounding the developmental challenges facing Southern Italy.

The impact of infrastructure deficits has been particularly pronounced in relation to public investment policies. <cite id="31d17040-1">Research demonstrates that "the collapse of public investment observable in Italy over the last decade has penalised southern regions disproportionally, considering these regions' much lower endowment of public infrastructures"</cite>. This analysis highlights how the structural characteristics of Southern Italy—its already disadvantaged starting position—make it particularly vulnerable to reductions in public investment, creating a feedback loop where underinvestment in infrastructure leads to persistent economic disadvantages.

More recent scholarship has examined specific policy approaches to addressing these infrastructure deficits, particularly focusing on the potential of Special Economic Zones (SEZs) as an industrial policy tool. Research has demonstrated that when these policies are properly implemented, they can be effective in reducing regional disparities. <cite id="31d17040-2">Studies of the Puglia region's SEZs show that "the presence of SEZs appears to positively influence regional development" and that "a positive impact that would not have materialized without the policy" has been documented through robust comparative analysis</cite>.

Beyond infrastructure investment, contemporary scholarship has increasingly emphasized the importance of coordinated territorial strategies that address the complex spatial dimensions of the North-South divide. <cite id="31d17040-0">Researchers have argued that "the South must think together and switch off over time" to achieve "critical mass in a strategic vision for the southern regional interconnected and relational system"</cite>. This perspective suggests that effective development policy requires overcoming the "atomization of interventions" that has characterized previous approaches and instead developing integrated strategies that address the interconnected nature of regional development challenges.

Current Perspectives and Future Directions

In recent years, Italian-language scholarship has moved beyond singular-factor explanations toward more comprehensive frameworks that recognize the complex, multidimensional nature of the North-South divide. Contemporary research increasingly emphasizes the importance of place-based policies that acknowledge the unique characteristics and historical contexts of Southern Italian regions rather than applying uniform national approaches. This shift reflects a growing recognition that effective development strategies must be tailored to the specific socioeconomic conditions, cultural contexts, and institutional capacities of individual southern regions.

The literature now more frequently addresses what scholars describe as the "triple divide" facing Italy's southern regions—the simultaneous existence of geographical, urban-rural, and coastal-inland gradients that all correlate with levels of economic development. This more nuanced spatial perspective has prompted researchers to develop more sophisticated analytical frameworks that can capture these complex spatial dynamics. <cite id="e046a23b-2">As noted by recent scholarship, "the spatial distribution of district value added" cannot be understood through "the traditional north-south axis alone," necessitating "at least two additional axes, the coastal-inland and the urban-rural gradients, as associated to the level of economic development"</cite>.

Contemporary Italian research also increasingly emphasizes the importance of regional specialization and comparative advantage as factors that can inform more effective development policies. Rather than viewing the South's economic structure as inherently inferior, this approach recognizes that different regions develop distinctive economic profiles based on their resource endowments, historical trajectories, and institutional contexts. This perspective has led to greater interest in how regional innovation systems in Southern Italy can be strengthened to support locally appropriate economic development paths.

The evolving scholarly consensus suggests that overcoming Southern Italy's economic lag will require integrated approaches that simultaneously address institutional quality, human capital formation, infrastructure deficits, and regional policy coherence. <cite id="e046a23b-2">As recent scholarship emphasizes, "designing 'one-size-fits-some' forms of national industrial policies" has proven ineffective, and instead, "place-based policies" that acknowledge "the key role of geography in shaping economic opportunities" offer a more promising path forward</cite>. This recognition represents a significant shift in emphasis within Italian-language scholarship, moving away from purely national or centralized approaches toward more localized strategies that can better address the specific challenges facing different parts of Southern Italy.</answer>

Title: European policies and domestic reform: a case study of structural fund management in Italy
Snippet: The challenge of overcoming the underdevelopment of the south of Italy (the Mezzogiorno, an area south of Rome comprising eight regions and over a third of the Italian population and therefore larger than some European countries) was one of the factors behind the extensive role played by the Italian state in that region's economy in the post-war period. From the mid-to late 1950s, the main task of fostering the industrialisation of the south was assigned to two institutions which became symbols of government policy for the south: the Cassa per il Mezzogiorno and the state-controlled companies and holdings. The Cassa per il Mezzogiorno ('Fund for the South'), was an independent agency, located outside the 'ordinary administration', which provided resources for public infrastructure works, public investments and incentives for private investment. In addition, the investment decisions of state-controlled companies as well as those controlled indirectly by the state (through the distinctive 'state holdings' formula) were directed heavily towards the south, and, from the late 1960s, indirect wage subsidies compensated for the high increases in (official) wages secured by the trade unions. 

The 'Italian model' of state intervention was initially not without success, especially in the context of Italy's 'economic miracle' which spanned much of the 1950s and 1960s. The principal state holdings companies (ENI and IRI) became much admired models of public enterprises and the lira was acclaimed for being one of the most stable currencies in Europe. 7 The difference in income between the south and centre-north was reduced and living conditions in the south improved significantly. These achievements, however, were short-lived, and in the period after the energy crisis in the early 1970s (which put intense pressure on the energyintensive and steel industry in the south), the state holding formula proved unable to cope with the seminal shift towards 'flexible specialisation' and entered into long-term financial crisis. Industrialisation of the south tended to create 'cathedrals in the desert': large state-backed industrialisation projects which failed to stimulate any spontaneous growth in local and regional economies around them.

Title: Italy’s North–South Economic Divide: Productivity Gaps, Institutional Quality, and the Persistence of Policy Failure
Snippet: Italy has traditionally had one of the longest regional economic separations between advanced economies with Northern regions rising above the South in productivity, employment and income levels. Regional convergence has become elusive even after decades of national development strategies and through massive European Union cohesion funding. The paper explores the economic and institutional origins of the North-South divide in Italy using a combination of regional gross domestic product data with a new regional panel dataset of institutional quality. The research focuses on the hypothesis that institutional quality differences, including corruption, government effectiveness, regulatory quality, rule of law and accountability can explain differences in productivity that persist across Italian regions using fixed-effects panel econometric methods. The findings reveal that the institutional quality has a statistically and economically significant impact on economic performance in regions, and significantly lower returns to institutional changes in the Southern regions. These results indicate that the failure of the policy in Italy cannot be simply attributed to the lack of investment but involves more profound structural and government-related issues. The paper has implications to the literature of regional development as it presents dynamic, sub-national data of the institution in terms of its influence on the long-run economic performance in one country.

Title: How do dimensions of institutional quality improve Italian regional innovation system efficiency? The Knowledge production function using SFA
Snippet: institutional quality indicators employed in the paper exhibit strong linear correlations. 16 According to Ariu et al. (2016), if the indices of governance exhibit strong linear correlations, it is then hard to empirically quantify their impact. Accordingly, the application of the PCA has the advantage to shrink the dimension of the governance indicators and to deal with the existing variability in the data. It is worth noting that in the literature that has investigated the impact of institutional quality upon efficiency, while Méon and Weill (2005) and Aldieri et al. (2020) have taken advantage of the full set of governance quality indicators identified by Kauffman et al. (2010), hence relying on a set of governance indices which is close to the one employed in this paper, the empirical analysis of Castiglione et al. (2018) only exploits the composite institutional quality indicator of Nifo and Vecchione (2014) and not just explores the potential contribution of each individual measure of institutional quality upon efficiency. All inputs and the output variables are in log-levels so that the overall positive skewness of the variables is reduced.

Descriptive statistics disaggregated by the four main Italian regional macroareas are reported in Table (2). What clearly emerges is the large dual structure of the Italian economy, which is visible not only considering the production function parameters, but also the variables related to the determinants of efficiency and the quality of institutions. Indeed, the descriptive statistics reveal that North-Western regions show a higher degree of economy activity, as signaled by the level of patents and R&D expenditures, while Southern regions 17 are characterised by a lower degree of R&D intensity, implying that regions in the North are the most innovative in the country. A similar picture emerges when considering the descriptive statistics related to the efficiency components, with North-Western regions which outperform all the others. Once again, the Southern part of the country registers the worst performance, displaying statistics which are indicative of an economy that did not achieve high levels of socio-economic development and a catching-up process with the most developed macro-areas of the country. 18 The same holds once we focus on the quality of regional institutions, with the Southern regions that exhibit weaker governance relatively to Center and Norther regions.

Title: No revenge of the places that don't matter? Evidence from Italy’s Cassa per il Mezzogiorno
Snippet: This institutional change that altered the funding course indicates an active role in reviving the Italian regional divide. As in prior periods of Italian economic history, the execution of an active modernisation process for Southern Italy favoured the re-emergence of endemic issues, trapping Southern Italy in underdevelopment and prompting a new approach to addressing developmental policies that were likely counterproductive to promoting regional convergence (Barone et al. 2016). This is in line with the evidence presented by Felice and Vasta (2015, p. 61) on the weak involvement of local institutions in that period. From the 1970s onwards, the engagement of local authorities in policymaking exacerbated the living conditions in Southern Italy and hindered economic growth. 

After the 1970s, the economic paradigm shifted, fostering scepticism towards direct economic intervention. In Italy, this shift triggered a heated debate about the activities of CasMez. Consequently, the regional disparity in Italy went out from the political agenda, leading to a substantial reduction in policies to foster regional convergence (Barca et al. 2012). The prevailing belief that CasMez was essentially a waste of resources that did not produce economic development in Southern Italy played a pivotal role in justifying this disengagement. It erected an ideological barrier to public intervention, especially in Southern Italy. The ascension of the right-wing Northern League party, which utilised anecdotal evidence to contend that fiscal resources were being squandered in Southern Italy, further entrenched this prevailing wisdom (Cento Bull 1993). Concurrently, a new player in regional policies emerged: the European Union's structural funds entrusted to local institutions. Regrettably, these policies did not substantially influence Southern Italy's growth; instead, they exacerbated corruption and nepotism (De Angelis et al. 2020;Di Cataldo and Mastrorocco 2022). The root cause of this failure can be traced back to the decentralisation of 1971, which became a persistent modus operandi in policy implementation and a problem for Southern Italy.

Title: The Dynamics of Fund Absorption: Evaluating the Efficacy of EU Structural Funds in Mitigating Regional Inequalities—Calabrian Case
Snippet: Historically, the migratory outflows from the Italian Mezzogiorno have shaped the socio-economic fabric of southern Italy.The 150-year timeline reveals a transition from the predominantly uneducated migrants of the early 20th century to the present-day exodus of educated young adults (Etzo 2011).This shift, particularly evident since the latter half of the 20th century, has been exacerbated by economic crises and a decrease in labor-intensive industries (Bonifazi et al. 2021).Since the 1990s, a resurgence in emigration has been noted, predominantly among those with secondary and higher education, propelled by disparate economic development between the southern regions and the more affluent central and northern Italy (Etzo 2011;Odoardi and Muratore 2019).Today's migratory flows are characterized by the internal and international relocation of individuals seeking superior educational and professional opportunities, contributing to a self-perpetuating cycle of territorial dualism and the enrichment of foreign labor markets at the expense of local development (Aronica et al. 2023;Basile et al. 2019).

The drivers of this migration are multifaceted, with educational and employment opportunities being primary motivators for those seeking regions where their skills are recognized and rewarded (Ferrara et al. 2018).The statistical narrative provided by the Instituto Nazionale di Statistica (ISTAT) for 2018 (ISTAT 2018) delineates a stark portrait of interregional transfers, signifying a substantial migration of the educated populace from the Mezzogiorno to more prosperous regions, further depleting the south's human capital (Statista 2019).

While labor mobility is traditionally seen as a mechanism for economic equilibrium, the Italian scenario deviates from this model due to the selective nature of the migration, which prioritizes highly qualified individuals.This selective emigration, as opposed to a homogenous distribution of workers, reinforces the dualistic nature of the Italian economy, exacerbating regional inequalities (Basile et al. 2019;Ballatore and Mariani 2019).The intervention of public policies has, paradoxically, not mitigated but seemingly intensified these disparities, perpetuating a negative cycle of talent outflow and contributing to the competitive advantage of the northern regions (Coniglio and Prota 2017).

Title: Brain gain versus brain drain: the effects of universities’ mobile students on territorial inequalities
Snippet: Between 2013 and 2019, an average of 24.7% of first-level graduates from southern universities enrolled in a master's degree in the Centre-North, while only 0.6% of graduates moved in the opposite direction. This graduate outflow phenomenon is especially relevant for southern regions' local development considering that a large share of these mobile students, once graduated, integrate into the local workforce (Alma-Laurea, 2021), strengthening the economy of the northern provinces (brain gain) while simultaneously depleting opportunities in the southern regions (brain drain). Consequently, student mobility exacerbates the enduring spatial disparities within Italy. 

Thus, a more specific research question is to investigate the spatial inequalities generated by student mobility. Accordingly, we analyse the impact of both incoming and outgoing students on the gross domestic product (GDP) per capita growth rate of Italian NUTS-3 regions. Furthermore, we assess whether the northern provinces benefit from a brain gain instead of a brain drain suffered by the southern areas due to student outflows. Lastly, we compute the additional contribution of student mobility to the existing income gap between the South and the Centre-North of Italy over the considered period. 

Another novelty of our analysis is that we focus on the mobility flows of students who have completed a first-level degree and chosen to pursue a second-level degree in a different Italian province. Section 3.1 provides a detailed definition of these mobile students. Unlike Ballarino et al. (2022), who examine first-level students, we concentrate on second-level students because they are closer to entering the labour market and, therefore, have a more immediate impact on the economic performance of the destination region (Dotti et al., 2013). 

The empirical model is based on a standard fixed effects growth model where the province's per capita GDP growth rate depends on the inflows and outflows of mobile students while controlling for other characteristics of the local economy, such as resident students, initial GDP conditions and population density. 

Our results show that in Italy incoming students have a notably positive and significant impact on the economic growth of the province where they study. This effect is especially pronounced in the Centre-North regions, where the influx of students contributes to a 'brain gain' phenomenon.

While labor mobility is traditionally seen as a mechanism for economic equilibrium, the Italian scenario deviates from this model due to the selective nature of the migration, which prioritizes highly qualified individuals.This selective emigration, as opposed to a homogenous distribution of workers, reinforces the dualistic nature of the Italian economy, exacerbating regional inequalities (Basile et al. 2019;Ballatore and Mariani 2019).The intervention of public policies has, paradoxically, not mitigated but seemingly intensified these disparities, perpetuating a negative cycle of talent outflow and contributing to the competitive advantage of the northern regions (Coniglio and Prota 2017).

snippet.text:
Between 2013 and 2019, an average of 24.7% of first-level graduates from southern universities enrolled in a master's degree in the Centre-North, while only 0.6% of graduates moved in the opposite direction. This graduate outflow phenomenon is especially relevant for southern regions' local development considering that a large share of these mobile students, once graduated, integrate into the local workforce (Alma-Laurea, 2021), strengthening the economy of the northern provinces (brain gain) while simultaneously depleting opportunities in the southern regions (brain drain). Consequently, student mobility exacerbates the enduring spatial disparities within Italy. 

Thus, a more specific research question is to investigate the spatial inequalities generated by student mobility. Accordingly, we analyse the impact of both incoming and outgoing students on the gross domestic product (GDP) per capita growth rate of Italian NUTS-3 regions. Furthermore, we assess whether the northern provinces benefit from a brain gain instead of a brain drain suffered by the southern areas due to student outflows. Lastly, we compute the additional contribution of student mobility to the existing income gap between the South and the Centre-North of Italy over the considered period. 

Another novelty of our analysis is that we focus on the mobility flows of students who have completed a first-level degree and chosen to pursue a second-level degree in a different Italian province. Section 3.1 provides a detailed definition of these mobile students. Unlike Ballarino et al. (2022), who examine first-level students, we concentrate on second-level students because they are closer to entering the labour market and, therefore, have a more immediate impact on the economic performance of the destination region (Dotti et al., 2013). 

The empirical model is based on a standard fixed effects growth model where the province's per capita GDP growth rate depends on the inflows and outflows of mobile students while controlling for other characteristics of the local economy, such as resident students, initial GDP conditions and population density. 

Our results show that in Italy incoming students have a notably positive and significant impact on the economic growth of the province where they study. This effect is especially pronounced in the Centre-North regions, where the influx of students contributes to a 'brain gain' phenomenon.

Title: A “Silent Revolution”: school reforms and Italy’s educational gender gap in the Liberal Age (1861–1921)
Snippet: Italy's economic growth in the long run is tightly linked to human capital accumulation. Vasta (1999) maintains that the remarkable delay in human capital accumulation has been a heavy toll on the country's capability to reach sustained growth in the long run and up to the present day (Di Martino and Vasta 2017). Indeed, the new stream of empirical quantitative studies in Italy's economic history has claimed that the aggregate stock of human capital is a main driver of industrial location (Basile andCiccarelli 2018, Missiaia 2018), innovation (Nuvolari and Vasta 2017), industrial growth (Cappelli 2017a) and the growth of real wages (Federico et al. 2019). 

Furthermore, schooling and education are crucial determinants of the long-term economic divergence between the North and the South of the country (Felice 2012;Felice and Vasta 2015). 

Due to this line of research, Italy's primary-school system during the Liberal Age and its relationship with education and human capital accumulation have been debated extensively, being mainly focused on the country's comparative human capital disadvantage and the educational North-South divide. Within the literature, there is a general agreement on the problematic nature of Italy's decentralized primary-school system (Felice and Vasta 2015;Cappelli 2017b), which hampered human capital accumulation, innovation and technological progress (Nuvolari andVasta 2015, 2017). As we explain in more detail below, the system established in 1859 set forth that funding and management of primary schooling was a burden on Italy's municipalities. New legislation on primary education in the first decade of the twentieth century-such as the Coppino or the Orlando Laws-produced a reduction in the literacy divide between North and South and prompted more rapid human capital formation; yet, amazingly, by 1911, average adult male literacy in the South was no higher than what it had been in Northern Italy in 1821 (Ciccarelli and Weisdorf 2019; Figure 7) and Italy lagged behind the educational performance of other countries. 

Two main interpretations have been provided on the determinants of such educational trends.

Title: Passive Modernization? The new Human Development Index and its components in Italy’s regions (1871-2007)
Snippet: The article presents and discusses estimates of social and economic indicators for Italy’s regions in benchmark years roughly from Unification to the present day: life expectancy, education, Gdp per capita at purchasing power parity, and the new Human Development Index (HDI). A broad interpretative hypothesis, based on the distinction between passive and active modernization, is proposed to account for the evolution of regional imbalances over the long-run. In the lack of active modernization, Southern Italy converged thanks to passive modernization, i.e., State intervention: however, this was more effective in life expectancy, less successful in education, expensive and as a whole ineffective in Gdp. As a consequence, convergence in the HDI occurred from the late XIX century to the 1970s, but came to a sudden halt in the last decades of the XX century.

Title: Between export-led growth and administrative Keynesianism: Italy’s two-tiered growth regime
Snippet: The second relates to the differentiated impact of European economic and monetary integration on countries with diverse regional growth regimes. Italy's experience suggests that northern Italy's export-led regions have managed to cope with greater global competition and a 'hard-currency' monetary regime in Europe. Indeed, as of 2022, Italy accounted 5 for 19 per cent of total EU industrial production, second only to Germany (at 26 per cent). Thus, thirty years after Richard Locke's writings (Locke 1995), Italy is still characterised by a dysfunctional national political economy hiding resilient patterns of regional economic dynamism. On the contrary, the sheltered AK regions of southern Italy have suffered disproportionately from the Eurozone's fiscal constraints and the austerity measures implemented after Italy's sovereign debt crisis. Given the key compensatory role played by public employment in AK regions, the public sector wage freezes and cuts implemented during 2009-2016(Di Carlo 2023) have eroded southern households' capacity to consume, further depressing regional demand and growth in AK regions. Likewise, the collapse of public investment observable in Italy over the last decade has penalised southern regions disproportionally, considering these regions' much lower endowment of public infrastructures (SVIMEZ 2023, p. XVI). Thus, taking regional growth regimes into account points to a more differentiated impact of European integration across heterogeneous territories within national models of capitalism. 

Thirdly, unearthing and understanding the structural differences across regions' growth regimes shall be instrumental for the design of place-based policies to avoid designing 'one-size-fits-some' forms of national industrial policies. Related to these aspects, through regional input-output data, future CPE research could also investigate the interlinkages between regional growth models to analyse intra-country patterns of regional trade and value chains and detect complementarities between regional growth regimes. 

Considering that the topic addressed in this article is politically contentious in Italy, we conclude by stressing that our analysis carries no normative judgement against southern Italy's 'subsidised' growth regime. Our aim was simply to analyse the ideal-typical characteristics of Italy's regional growth regimes.

Title: Are Special Economic Zone policies (SEZ) effective? An empirical analysis on the transport and logistics’ sector
Snippet: To attract investment, stimulate economic growth, and generate employment, many countries have established SEZs. These areas offer fiscal benefits and receive financial, infrastructural, and logistical support while governed by special legislation and streamlined procedures distinct from other parts of the country. Generally, these zones have proven to be effective industrial policy tools, driving economic growth at both national and local levels. However, their success ultimately hinges on the long-term objectives of the associated industrial policies (Arbolino, Lantz, and Napolitano 2023). Aligning instruments such as the SEZs in Southern Italy with the substantial resources provided by the PNRR could represent a strategic combination capable of reducing productive and social disparities between the South and the more developed central-northern regions (Di Berardino et al. 2016). 

Previous studies have highlighted that the SEZs in Puglia have destinated significant resources into transport and logistics (Nisticò and Prota 2023). Although the literature acknowledges that policy impacts vary by region and, in some cases, have a very limited impact on firms in the service sector (Frick and Rodríguez-Pose 2022;Rodríguez-Pose et al. 2022), this analysis of Puglia offers counterintuitive results demonstrating that effective integration of SEZ policies is heavily dependent on the local economic context. Our findings reveal that the introduction of SEZs in Puglia has led to an increase of more than 10% on average in the turnover of transport sector companies. These results highlight the significance of industrial policy and support the ongoing evolution of SEZ policy in Italy, which is culminating in the establishment of a unified SEZ for the South of Italy. Under this new model, previously limited to select territories, fiscal and administrative benefits will be accessible to all companies in the Southern Regions. 

Additionally, this study enhances the understanding of the link between SEZs and regional growth in Italy. For Puglia, the presence of SEZs appears to positively influence regional development. It also addresses scepticism regarding the effectiveness of SEZs. By employing a robust control group, we demonstrate a positive impact that would not have materialized without the policy, offering encouraging evidence for policymakers about the effectiveness of SEZs.

snippet.text:
The second relates to the differentiated impact of European economic and monetary integration on countries with diverse regional growth regimes. Italy's experience suggests that northern Italy's export-led regions have managed to cope with greater global competition and a 'hard-currency' monetary regime in Europe. Indeed, as of 2022, Italy accounted 5 for 19 per cent of total EU industrial production, second only to Germany (at 26 per cent). Thus, thirty years after Richard Locke's writings (Locke 1995), Italy is still characterised by a dysfunctional national political economy hiding resilient patterns of regional economic dynamism. On the contrary, the sheltered AK regions of southern Italy have suffered disproportionately from the Eurozone's fiscal constraints and the austerity measures implemented after Italy's sovereign debt crisis. Given the key compensatory role played by public employment in AK regions, the public sector wage freezes and cuts implemented during 2009-2016(Di Carlo 2023) have eroded southern households' capacity to consume, further depressing regional demand and growth in AK regions. Likewise, the collapse of public investment observable in Italy over the last decade has penalised southern regions disproportionally, considering these regions' much lower endowment of public infrastructures (SVIMEZ 2023, p. XVI). Thus, taking regional growth regimes into account points to a more differentiated impact of European integration across heterogeneous territories within national models of capitalism. 

Thirdly, unearthing and understanding the structural differences across regions' growth regimes shall be instrumental for the design of place-based policies to avoid designing 'one-size-fits-some' forms of national industrial policies. Related to these aspects, through regional input-output data, future CPE research could also investigate the interlinkages between regional growth models to analyse intra-country patterns of regional trade and value chains and detect complementarities between regional growth regimes. 

Considering that the topic addressed in this article is politically contentious in Italy, we conclude by stressing that our analysis carries no normative judgement against southern Italy's 'subsidised' growth regime. Our aim was simply to analyse the ideal-typical characteristics of Italy's regional growth regimes.

snippet.text:
To attract investment, stimulate economic growth, and generate employment, many countries have established SEZs. These areas offer fiscal benefits and receive financial, infrastructural, and logistical support while governed by special legislation and streamlined procedures distinct from other parts of the country. Generally, these zones have proven to be effective industrial policy tools, driving economic growth at both national and local levels. However, their success ultimately hinges on the long-term objectives of the associated industrial policies (Arbolino, Lantz, and Napolitano 2023). Aligning instruments such as the SEZs in Southern Italy with the substantial resources provided by the PNRR could represent a strategic combination capable of reducing productive and social disparities between the South and the more developed central-northern regions (Di Berardino et al. 2016). 

Previous studies have highlighted that the SEZs in Puglia have destinated significant resources into transport and logistics (Nisticò and Prota 2023). Although the literature acknowledges that policy impacts vary by region and, in some cases, have a very limited impact on firms in the service sector (Frick and Rodríguez-Pose 2022;Rodríguez-Pose et al. 2022), this analysis of Puglia offers counterintuitive results demonstrating that effective integration of SEZ policies is heavily dependent on the local economic context. Our findings reveal that the introduction of SEZs in Puglia has led to an increase of more than 10% on average in the turnover of transport sector companies. These results highlight the significance of industrial policy and support the ongoing evolution of SEZ policy in Italy, which is culminating in the establishment of a unified SEZ for the South of Italy. Under this new model, previously limited to select territories, fiscal and administrative benefits will be accessible to all companies in the Southern Regions. 

Additionally, this study enhances the understanding of the link between SEZs and regional growth in Italy. For Puglia, the presence of SEZs appears to positively influence regional development. It also addresses scepticism regarding the effectiveness of SEZs. By employing a robust control group, we demonstrate a positive impact that would not have materialized without the policy, offering encouraging evidence for policymakers about the effectiveness of SEZs.
